passages.happening:
Outside the garden, life goes on. Eve gives birth to a son, Cain, and says, “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man” (verse 1). Then she has a second son, Abel. Abel keeps sheep. Cain farms the soil (verse 2).

In time both brothers bring an offering to the LORD. Cain brings “some of the fruit of the soil” (verse 3). Abel brings “the best portions of the firstborn of his flock” (verse 4). God looks with favor on Abel and his offering, “but He had no regard for Cain and his offering” (verse 5).

Cain becomes very angry, and his face falls. God speaks to him before anything worse happens. He asks why Cain is angry. He tells him that if he does what is right, he will be accepted. Then comes a warning: “sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Hebrew listeners would hear the names. Cain (Qayin) sounds like the verb Eve uses, ‘I have brought forth’ or ‘I have gotten’ (qanah). Abel (Hevel) is the ordinary Hebrew word for a breath or a vapor, the word that runs through Ecclesiastes. The story never comments on it, but a Hebrew reader would feel it: this is the brother whose life will vanish like a breath.

Farming and herding were the two great ways of making a living in the ancient world. Both were honest work. The brothers each bring the fruit of their own labor, and neither kind of gift is wrong in itself. Israel's later law welcomed offerings of grain as well as animals (Leviticus 2).

The words for Abel's gift would catch the ear. He brings the ‘firstborn’, the first and best, and the ‘fat portions’. In Israel's law the fat was the part kept for God: “All the fat is the LORD’s” (Leviticus 3:16). Cain's gift is described more plainly, as ‘some of’ his crops.

Notice also the warning in verse 7. This is the first time the Bible uses the word ‘sin’. It is pictured like an animal lying in wait at the door. And the words for ‘desire’ and ‘master’ are the same two words used to the woman in 3:16. The struggle that broke the first marriage now crouches outside the first son's door.
passages.later:
The New Testament gives two answers about the brothers that help with this passage. Hebrews says, “By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did” (Hebrews 11:4). John says Cain killed his brother “Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous” (1 John 3:12). Both point to the heart of the giver, not only to the gift.

The warning about anger runs through Scripture. The psalm says, “Be angry, yet do not sin” (Psalm 4:4), and Paul repeats it, adding, “Do not let the sun set upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). Jesus traces murder back to the angry heart: “anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment” (Matthew 5:22).

The prophets also say that God looks past the gift to the giver. When Samuel looks at outward appearances, God tells him, “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.hard:
Why did God accept Abel's offering and not Cain's? The text does not say. Readers have given several answers, and more than one may be true.

Some point to the gifts themselves. Abel brought the first and best of his flock. Cain brought ‘some’ of his crops, with no word that it was his first or best. On this reading, the difference is wholehearted giving and half-hearted giving.

Others point to the givers. Hebrews says Abel gave ‘by faith’, and 1 John says Cain's deeds were evil. On this reading, God saw what was already in each brother's heart. Cain's anger in verse 5 shows what was there.

Some have said that only an animal sacrifice could please God. But Israel's law gladly received grain offerings, so many readers doubt that this was the point.

Others note a pattern that runs through Genesis: God often chooses the younger brother over the elder, by his own free choice and not by birth order. Abel, and later Seth, stand first in that line.

What the text does make plain is that Cain was not rejected for good. God came to him, spoke kindly, and told him the way was still open: ‘If you do what is right, will you not be accepted?’
passages.asks: God speaks to Cain before the crime, not only after it. Ask where anger or envy is crouching at your own door, and whether you are mastering it or feeding it. Then ask what you bring to God: the first and best, or whatever is left over.

passages.happening:
Cain speaks to Abel and says, “Let us go out to the field.” There, Cain rises up against his brother and kills him (verse 8).

God comes with a question, as he did in the garden: “Where is your brother Abel?” Cain lies: “I do not know!” Then he adds, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (verse 9).

God answers, “What have you done?” Then he says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (verse 10). The ground that received Abel's blood will no longer give its crops to Cain. He will be “a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth” (verse 12).

Cain protests that his punishment is more than he can bear. He fears that whoever finds him will kill him (verses 13-14). God answers, “Not so” and puts a mark on Cain “so that no one who found him would kill him” (verse 15). Cain goes out from the presence of the LORD and settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
In the standard Hebrew text, verse 8 does not say what Cain said to Abel. It reads as if the words have dropped out. The Samaritan copy of the Torah, the ancient Greek translation and others supply the words ‘Let us go out to the field’, and many modern Bibles follow them.

Cain's question has a sting in it. The word ‘keeper’ comes from the Hebrew verb shamar, to keep or guard. It is the same verb used when God put the man in the garden ‘to keep it’ (2:15). Human beings were made to keep and care. Cain throws the word back at God with a shrug.

In the ancient world, a murder was answered by the dead man's family. The nearest relative was expected to take a life for a life. Israel's law later called him “the avenger of blood” (Numbers 35:19). Cain's fear that someone will kill him comes from that world of blood feud.

So the mark is surprising. Cain is the murderer, yet God protects him. The word for ‘mark’ is ot, a sign. Genesis uses the same word for the rainbow (9:12) and for circumcision (17:11). It is a sign of God's protection. The text never says what it looked like.

‘Nod’ means ‘wandering’. It sounds like the word for the ‘wanderer’ Cain was told he would be. Cain settles in the land of wandering. Like his parents, he goes east, further from Eden.
passages.later:
Jesus names Abel as the first in a long line of innocent people killed: “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35). Hebrews says that Abel ‘still speaks, even though he is dead’ (Hebrews 11:4).

Hebrews also sets Abel's blood beside the blood of Jesus. Believers have come “to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel's blood cried out for justice. Christ's blood speaks forgiveness.

John uses Cain as a warning to the church: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Jude speaks of false teachers who “have traveled the path of Cain” (Jude 1:11).

And the cry of innocent blood is not forgotten. In Revelation the souls of those who were killed for God's word cry out, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?” (Revelation 6:10). God hears blood that no one else hears.
passages.hard:
What was the mark of Cain? The text does not say what it looked like, only what it was for: to keep Cain alive. It was a mark of mercy, not of shame.

In nineteenth-century America some churches taught that Cain's mark was black skin and used that claim to defend slavery and to keep Black people out of church office; that teaching is false and evil, and these notes reject it. The text says nothing about skin or race. In Genesis every human being is made in God's image (1:27, 9:6).

A word of care for two kinds of readers. If you carry guilt for harm you have done, notice how God treats Cain. He does not pretend the murder did not happen. Cain lives with what he did. But God still speaks to him, still listens to him, and still protects his life. Your story is not over. Tell the truth about it to God and to someone you trust, a pastor or a counsellor, and where it is possible and safe, make it right. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

If you have lost someone to violence, notice that God hears the blood that cries from the ground. Your grief and your longing for justice are not wrong. Scripture gives you words for them. Please do not carry this alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
passages.asks: God asks Cain two questions: ‘Where is your brother?’ and ‘What have you done?’ Ask who God has put in your care, and whether you have treated them as your brother or sister. Then notice that God protects even a murderer. Ask whether you are willing to want mercy for someone who has done great wrong.

passages.happening:
Cain has a son, Enoch, and builds a city named after him (verse 17). The man told he would wander builds a place to stay.

The family line runs on to Lamech, six generations after Adam through Cain (verse 18). Lamech marries two women, Adah and Zillah (verse 19). Their sons begin the arts of life. Jabal is the father of those who live in tents and raise livestock. Jubal is “the father of all who play the harp and flute.” Tubal-cain is “a forger of every implement of bronze and iron” (verses 20-22).

Then Lamech sings a short poem to his wives: “I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would notice how much good comes from this line. Cities, herding, music and metalwork are real gifts. Genesis says these arts began with ordinary human beings, and in the family of a murderer. Skill and beauty are good gifts of God, but they do not make anyone good.

Lamech is the first man in the Bible said to have two wives. Genesis does not stop to say this is wrong. It often reports what people do and lets the story show the results. The pattern of one man and one woman in chapter 2 has already been broken.

Lamech's words are a poem, and a terrible one. God protected Cain with a promise of sevenfold vengeance, to stop the killing. Lamech turns that mercy into a boast. He kills a young man for a blow and claims vengeance without limit. In a few generations, the line of Cain has gone from one murder with fear to killing as a song.
passages.later:
Jesus answers Lamech's song. Peter asks how many times he must forgive his brother, “Up to seven times?” Jesus says, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:21-22). In the Greek translation of Genesis, Lamech's ‘seventy-sevenfold’ uses the same rare Greek word that Jesus uses here. Many readers hear Jesus turning Lamech's endless revenge into endless forgiveness.

Paul tells believers, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19). Vengeance belongs to God, who judges justly. It is not for a Lamech to take without limit.

The good gifts of Cain's line, music and craft, are taken up in God's service later. Bezalel is filled with skill to work gold, silver and bronze for the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3-5), and the last psalm calls God's people to “praise Him with strings and flute” (Psalm 150:4).
passages.hard:
Where did Cain's wife come from? And who built the city with him? The chapter does not stop to explain. Genesis says that Adam and Eve “had other sons and daughters” (5:4).

The oldest and most common answer is that Cain married a sister, or a niece. An ancient Jewish retelling of Genesis, the Book of Jubilees (from about the second century BC), already says so. On this view the early family grew over long lives, and marriage between close relatives was not yet forbidden, as it later was in Israel's law (Leviticus 18:9).

Others think the chapter seems to assume more people outside Adam's family, since Cain fears strangers and builds a city. Some Christians who read Adam and Eve as a real couple hold that other people were living at the time. Others read these chapters as a story about humanity told through one family.

The text says what it says (5:4) and leaves the rest unexplained. Its interest lies elsewhere: in what sin does between brothers, and in how God answers it.
passages.asks: Lamech took God's mercy and turned it into a license for revenge. Ask whether you keep score, and whether you want to pay back more than you received. Then ask what Jesus' ‘seventy-seven times’ would mean in the one relationship where forgiving is hardest for you.

passages.t: Seth, and calling on the LORD
passages.happening:
Adam and Eve have another son. Eve names him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him” (verse 25).

Seth has a son, Enosh. And the chapter closes with a quiet sentence: “At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The name Seth sounds like the Hebrew verb ‘granted’ or ‘appointed’ in Eve's words. She does not forget Abel. She names her new son in his memory. A mother's grief stands inside the joy.

Notice her word ‘seed’. It is the word of the promise in 3:15, that the woman's seed would crush the serpent. One seed has been killed, and the other has become a murderer. But God gives another. The promise is not lost.

The chapter has set two lines side by side. Cain's line builds a city and ends in Lamech's boast of violence. Seth's line begins with a short notice of worship. To ‘call upon the name of the LORD’ means to pray to him and worship him by name. Abraham will do the same at his altars (12:8).

Enosh, like Adam, is also a Hebrew word for a human being, a mortal man. The line that calls on God's name begins with a name that means ‘mortal’.
passages.later:
The prophets take up the words of verse 26 as a promise. Joel says, “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32). Peter quotes it on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:21), and Paul quotes it in Romans: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). What began in the days of Enosh becomes the open door for every nation.

Luke traces Jesus' family line back through this very family: “the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38).
passages.asks: In a chapter full of anger and blood, the last word is prayer. Ask what it would look like for you to ‘call upon the name of the LORD’ in the middle of whatever violence or grief surrounds you. And notice that Eve could name her joy and her loss in one breath. Ask whether you let your prayers hold both.
